title: Death promises the teaching: the fire hidden in the cave
theme: Yama promises to teach the fire that leads to heaven, which brings the endless world and is the support of all, hidden in the cave.

words.gram: pres. act. participle m. nom. sg.
words.context: Śaṅkara: «प्रजानन् विज्ञातवान्सन्नहमित्यर्थः» — I, who know it

words.meaning: the attaining of the endless world

words.context: Śaṅkara: «विदुषां बुद्धौ निविष्टमित्यर्थः» — in the intellect of the wise

sandhi.rule: Final t before a vowel becomes d: P. 8.2.39 (झलां जशोऽन्ते).
Final m stays before a vowel.

samasa.meaning: the attaining of the endless world; Śaṅkara: the means of reaching heaven

morphology.note: The preverb pra is separated from its verb by the enclitic te (tmesis), as Vedic allows; Raṅgarāmānuja cites P. 1.4.82 (व्यवहिताश्च).
Present participle of pra-jñā. Raṅgarāmānuja explains the suffix by P. 3.2.126 (लक्षणहेत्वोः क्रियायाः) as expressing a cause: ‘because I know it’.
atha + u; as a particle ending in o it is pragṛhya (P. 1.1.15 ओत्), though here it stands before a consonant.

translation.literal: ‘I declare [it] to you — learn it from me, I who know well the fire that leads to heaven, O Naciketas. Know this [fire] as the attaining of the endless world and the foundation, hidden in the cave.’
translation.readable: ‘I will tell you — listen and learn from me, Naciketas, for I know that heavenly fire well. Know that it wins the endless world, that it is the ground of all, and that it lies hidden in the cave of the heart.’

syntax: Two sentences. The first is a promise (pra te bravīmi, tad u me nibodha) with the participle prajānan giving Yama’s qualification. The second (viddhi tvam etam …) gives the fire three predicates: the attaining of the endless world, the foundation, hidden in the cave.

ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara: the fire, as known in the intellect of the wise: «निहितं स्थितं गुहायाम् । विदुषां बुद्धौ निविष्टमित्यर्थः». Madhva: it is Viṣṇu in the heart of all, «स विष्णुस्सर्वहृ», and Vedeśatīrtha argues against Śaṅkara’s gloss that the cave must mean the heart, as it does later in the text.

ambiguities.topic: anantaloka: the endless world, or Ananta’s world?
ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara: the means to the fruit of the heaven-world. Raṅgarāmānuja: the world of Ananta, Viṣṇu, «विष्णोः लोकः, तत्प्राप्तिम्». Madhva’s verse gives both: «लोको विष्णोरनन्तस्य तज्ज्ञानान्नित्य आप्यते».

beginner: Yama agrees to teach the fire. Listen and learn from me, he says, for I know it well. Then he praises it: this fire wins the endless world, it is the ground on which the world rests, and it is hidden in the cave. The cave is a famous image in the Kaṭha: a hidden inner place, which later in the Upaniṣad is where the self dwells. Here it already hints that the fire is not only bricks and flame; it is also something understood within. The commentators disagree on what exactly is hidden, but all agree that the teaching has an inner side.
analogy: Like a map that shows a road on paper but can only be followed by someone who has understood it inwardly.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: To teach the fire, which he knows well; he praises it as the attaining of the endless world, the foundation, and hidden in the cave.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara: the words are to settle the student’s mind: «प्रब्रवीमि तन्निबोधेति च शिष्यबुद्धिसमाधानार्थं वचनम्». The fire is the support of the world as Virāj: «प्रतिष्ठाम् आश्रयं जगतो विराट्स्वरूपेण».

commentary.q: What does Madhva see in the fire?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Madhva’s own verse: the fire is Hari, named Agni for being foremost («अग्यत्वादग्निनामाऽसौ» in the digital text, for agryatvāt), and the world of the endless Viṣṇu is reached by knowing him: «लोको विष्णोरनन्तस्य तज्ज्ञानान्नित्य आप्यते»; he is the support of all the worlds, «प्रतिष्ठा सर्वलोकस्य».

commentary.q: How does Raṅgarāmānuja read ‘the endless world’?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: As Viṣṇu’s world, citing ‘that highest step of Viṣṇu’ later in the Kaṭha: «विष्णोः लोकः, तत्प्राप्तिम्», and the foundation as non-return, «अपुनरावृत्तिं च».

advaita.text: The fire is praised as the means to heaven and as Virāj, the support of the world; ‘hidden in the cave’ means known in the minds of the wise: «विदुषां बुद्धौ निविष्टमित्यर्थः».

visistadvaita.text: The fire, known as part of meditation on Brahman, leads to Viṣṇu’s world and to non-return: «विष्णोः लोकः, तत्प्राप्तिम्».

dvaita.text: The fire named here is Hari, «अग्यत्वादग्निनामाऽसौ», and the cave is every being’s heart. Vedeśatīrtha rejects reading the endless world as heaven: «स्वर्गलोकस्यानन्तलोकत्वाभावात्».

schools.disagreement: Śaṅkara keeps the fire a ritual means to heaven (and to identity with Virāj); Raṅgarāmānuja and Madhva see the Lord behind it, and the endless world as Viṣṇu’s, not heaven. The ‘cave’ is the wise man’s intellect for Śaṅkara, the heart for the Mādhva commentators.

parallels.note: The Taittirīya’s ‘hidden in the cave, in the highest space’ says the same of Brahman: the phrase belongs to the shared language of the Upaniṣads for what is present but unseen.

contemporary.text: A procedure can be learnt by rote, but Yama says this one is ‘hidden in the cave’: understood within. Many skills are like that — what makes them work cannot be shown, only understood. (A modern reflection.)

reflect.beginner: What do you know how to do that you could not fully explain to someone else?
reflect.deeper: Why would a ritual be said to be ‘hidden in the cave’?
reflect.practice: Repeat a familiar task slowly today, and notice what you understand about it that is not in any instruction.

flags.note: The digital text of Madhva’s verse reads अग्यत्वाद् (for अग्र्यत्वाद्, ‘for being foremost’, as the commentators explain); quoted as printed.
